claims.statement: Synchronous code runs on the current call stack and runs to completion before queued callbacks can run.
A top-level script is itself executed as a task.
After the current task finishes and the stack is empty, the event loop drains the entire microtask queue.
Promise.then callbacks are queued as microtasks, even when the promise is already resolved.
queueMicrotask(callback) directly adds callback to the microtask queue.
setTimeout(..., 0) schedules a timer callback as a task; zero means eligible as soon as possible, not immediate.
The usual ordering is: synchronous logs, all queued microtasks, then the next eligible task such as a timer callback.
Microtasks added while draining the microtask queue run before the event loop starts the next task.

misconceptionsToAddress: Code runs top to bottom including timer and Promise callbacks without queue boundaries.
Promises and timers are the same generic kind of asynchronous work.
setTimeout(..., 0) runs immediately after the synchronous statement that scheduled it.
A Promise.then callback can run synchronously when the promise is already resolved.
The event loop runs only one microtask and then moves to the next task.
